reference.source: Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics / GeneReviews mitochondrial disease
clinicalPearls: The defining tetrad is myoclonus, generalised epilepsy, cerebellar ataxia and a myopathy with ragged-red fibres on muscle biopsy
Most cases are due to the maternally inherited m.8344A>G point mutation in the MT-TK gene encoding the mitochondrial transfer RNA for lysine
As with other mitochondrial tRNA disorders, heteroplasmy and a threshold effect explain the variable severity and age of onset across a maternal lineage
Additional features may include sensorineural deafness, optic atrophy, peripheral neuropathy, dementia and multiple symmetrical lipomatosis of the neck and trunk
Elevated resting or exercise-induced lactate supports the diagnosis but is neither universal nor specific
Myoclonus is frequently stimulus-sensitive and can be difficult to control; some anticonvulsants worsen mitochondrial function and are best avoided
Muscle histochemistry shows ragged-red fibres that are typically cytochrome c oxidase deficient, reflecting the tRNA translation defect
reference.pathophysiology: MERRF is caused by a mitochondrial tRNA mutation, usually m.8344A>G in MT-TK, that impairs mitochondrial translation and thereby the synthesis of respiratory-chain subunits, reducing oxidative phosphorylation capacity. The mutation is maternally inherited and heteroplasmic, so clinical expression depends on the proportion of mutant genomes and the energy threshold of each tissue. Neurons of the cerebellum, brainstem and cerebral cortex, together with skeletal muscle, are especially vulnerable to the resulting energy deficit, producing the characteristic myoclonus, seizures, ataxia and myopathy. Accumulation of abnormal mitochondria beneath the sarcolemma gives the ragged-red appearance on trichrome staining.
additionalDifferentials: Other progressive myoclonic epilepsies such as Unverricht-Lundborg and Lafora disease
additionalInvestigations: Resting and post-exercise blood lactate and pyruvate
Electroencephalography to characterise generalised epileptiform and photosensitive discharges
Brain MRI, which may show cerebellar and brainstem atrophy or basal ganglia calcification
Targeted molecular testing for m.8344A>G with heteroplasmy quantification in appropriate tissue
Skeletal muscle biopsy for ragged-red fibres and respiratory-chain enzymology
Audiometry and nerve conduction studies for associated deafness and neuropathy
redFlags: Poorly controlled myoclonic seizures or status epilepticus
Rapid neurological deterioration or new cardiorespiratory compromise
Cardiac conduction abnormality or cardiomyopathy on surveillance
Metabolic decompensation with rising lactic acidosis
reference.prognosis: MERRF is slowly progressive with a broad spectrum of severity; many patients have a normal early childhood before symptoms emerge, but accumulating myoclonus, ataxia and dementia can be disabling, and lifespan may be reduced in severely affected individuals.
pitfalls: Labelling the disorder an idiopathic progressive myoclonic epilepsy without pursuing mitochondrial testing
Relying on blood alone for genetic testing, since low-level heteroplasmy may be missed
Prescribing anticonvulsants that impair respiratory-chain or mitochondrial function
Overlooking cardiac and audiological involvement that warrants surveillance
management: Antiepileptic therapy for seizures and myoclonus, favouring agents such as levetiracetam and clonazepam while avoiding sodium valproate, which is mitochondrially toxic
Supportive mitochondrial supplementation such as coenzyme Q10, riboflavin and L-carnitine, recognising the limited evidence base
Management of complications including hearing aids or cochlear implantation for sensorineural deafness and rehabilitation for cerebellar ataxia
Avoidance of mitochondrial toxins including aminoglycosides and valproate
Surveillance for cardiac conduction disease, endocrinopathy and progressive neurological decline
Physiotherapy, occupational therapy and multidisciplinary neurological support
Genetic counselling emphasising maternal mitochondrial inheritance and heteroplasmy, with assessment of the maternal lineage
